description_ru: Антиквар и покупательница торгуются из-за часов с сомнительным происхождением. Каждая реплика скрывает подвох.
text:
Fenwick: Ah, madam, you have an eye. That clock is a Regency mantel piece, circa 1815, in original working order.
Oakes: It says seven minutes past four, and it is a quarter to two.
Fenwick: It keeps its own time. Many of the finest pieces do. One must meet them halfway.
Oakes: I should prefer a clock that meets me. What is the provenance?
Fenwick: Provenance. Yes. A distinguished one. It belonged, I am told, to a lady of considerable breeding.
Oakes: Told by whom?
Fenwick: By the lady's nephew. Who, I should say, had a very honest face.
Oakes: I find that the faces of nephews are rarely the most reliable evidence. Why is the back panel screwed down with modern screws?
Fenwick: Preservation. The original fastenings were, ah, not up to the task.
Oakes: Mr. Fenwick, the screws are stamped with the name of a supermarket.
Fenwick: A supermarket with exceptional ironmongery. Now, madam, I have other buyers who are most keen. A gentleman was in only this morning.
Oakes: Was he, by any chance, your nephew?
Fenwick: I am an only child.
Oakes: A tragic fact, though it does explain the confidence.
Oakes: Of course. Let me be plain. I am a retired horologist. I spent forty years restoring clocks for the National Trust, and I can tell a Regency movement from a Tuesday afternoon in Birmingham.
Fenwick: I see. And what, in your expert opinion, is this?
Oakes: A Victorian case, with a Continental movement from about 1890, and a dial that was repainted last week.
Fenwick: Last week? Surely not.
Oakes: It is still faintly tacky, Mr. Fenwick, and it smells of enamel.
Fenwick: Perhaps the previous owner liked to keep it fresh.
Oakes: The previous owner, I suspect, was you, on Thursday, with a small brush and a radio playing.
Fenwick: It is a very old enamel.
Oakes: It is a very fresh one. However. I should like to buy it.
Fenwick: You would? That is, I mean, naturally. I would not dream of parting with it for less than four hundred pounds.
Oakes: Eighty.
Fenwick: Madam, that is an insult to the craftsman.
Oakes: The craftsman, if he exists, was probably paid forty. I shall say one hundred and twenty, on condition that you tell me where the movement really came from.
Fenwick: It came from a house clearance in Dorchester. A very sad house. Seven cats.
Oakes: And the lady of breeding?
Fenwick: Possibly one of the cats.
Oakes: I see. A dynasty of cats, then, and a clock that has outlived them all.
Oakes: That is the first honest thing you have said all afternoon. One hundred and fifty, and I shall not mention the supermarket screws.
Fenwick: Done. You drive a hard bargain, Mrs. Oakes.
Oakes: I drive a soft one, Mr. Fenwick. I could have reported you to Trading Standards.
Fenwick: I shall wrap it in my best tissue paper. May I ask why you want it? It is, frankly, a fraud.
Oakes: It is a very good fraud. Somebody put real affection into that dial. I should like to see it run.
Fenwick: Well. I suppose that is the most flattering thing anyone has said about my stock.
Oakes: Do not let it go to your head. You still owe me a receipt, a guarantee, and an apology to the cats.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: aɪ: начинайте с открытого «а» и скользите к «и»; не сокращайте до «ай» с йотой: time, finest.
ɒ: короткий, губы слегка округлены, рот открыт; в американском варианте ближе к «а»: clock, honest.
Ударение: PROV-e-nance, ho-ROL-o-gist, pres-er-VA-tion; суффиксы -tion и -ist смещают ударение.
Конечное l твёрдое: кончик языка к дёснам и задняя спинка поднята; не «ль»: old, real.

questions.question: What does the clock actually show?
What is Mrs. Oakes's former profession?
Where did the movement really come from?
What price do they agree on?
